title: Part 2, Chapter 64
paragraphs: About the adventure that gave Don Quixote more unhappiness than anything that had so far befallen him

Don Antonio Moreno's wife, so the history tells us, was extremely happy to see Ana Felix in her house. She welcomed her with great kindness, charmed by her beauty as much as by her intelligence — for in both respects the fair Morisco was richly endowed, and all the people of the city flocked to see her as though they had been summoned by the ringing of the bells.

Don Quixote told Don Antonio that the plan they had adopted for rescuing Don Gregorio was not a good one, since its risks were greater than its rewards, and it would be better for himself to land in Barbary with his arms and his horse; for he would carry him off in spite of the whole Moorish host, as Don Gaiferos carried off his wife Melisendra.

"Remember, your worship," Sancho observed on hearing him say this, "Señor Don Gaiferos carried off his wife from the mainland and took her to France by land; but in this case, if by chance we carry off Don Gregorio, we have no way of getting him to Spain — because there's the sea in between."
"There's a remedy for everything except death," said Don Quixote; "if they bring the vessel close to the shore we'll be able to get on board, though all the world try to prevent us."

"Your worship hits it off mightily well and mightily easy," said Sancho; "but 'it's a long step from saying to doing,' and I stick with the renegade, for he seems to me an honest, good-hearted fellow."

Don Antonio then said that if the renegade did not succeed, the alternative of the great Don Quixote's expedition to Barbary would be adopted. Two days later the renegade put to sea in a light vessel of six oars a side manned by a stout crew, and two days after that the galleys made sail eastward — the general having asked the viceroy to let him know all about the release of Don Gregorio and about Ana Felix, and the viceroy promised to do so.

One morning as Don Quixote went out for a stroll along the beach in full armour (for, as he often said, that was "his only gear, his only rest the fray," and he was never without it for a moment), he saw coming towards him a knight, also in full armour, with a shining moon painted on his shield. When the knight had come near enough to be heard, he said in a loud voice, addressing Don Quixote, "Illustrious knight, never sufficiently extolled Don Quixote of La Mancha, I am the Knight of the White Moon, whose unheard-of achievements will perhaps have recalled me to your memory. I have come to do battle with you and prove the might of your arm, with the aim of making you acknowledge and confess that my lady, whoever she may be, is incomparably fairer than your Dulcinea del Toboso. If you acknowledge this fairly and openly, you shall escape death and save me the trouble of inflicting it on you. If you fight and I defeat you, I demand no other satisfaction than this: that you lay aside your arms, give up going in quest of adventures, withdraw, and retire to your own village for the space of a year, to live there without putting hand to sword, in peace and quiet and beneficial repose, the same being needful for the increase of your estate and the salvation of your soul; and if you defeat me, my head shall be at your disposal, my arms and horse your spoils, and the renown of my deeds transferred and added to yours. Consider which will be your best course, and give me your answer quickly, for this day is all the time I have for the business."

Don Quixote was amazed and astonished both at the Knight of the White Moon's arrogance and at his reason for delivering the challenge, and with calm dignity he answered him, "Knight of the White Moon, of whose achievements I have never heard until now, I would venture to swear you have never seen the illustrious Dulcinea; for had you seen her, I know you would have taken care not to risk yourself on this issue, because the sight would have removed all doubt from your mind that there ever has been or could be a beauty to compare with hers. So, not saying you lie, but only that you are mistaken in what you state, I accept your challenge on the conditions you have proposed, and at once — so that the day you have set does not run out. From your conditions I except only that of the renown of your deeds being transferred to me, since I know nothing of what sort they are or what they may amount to; I am content with my own, such as they may be. So take whichever side of the field you prefer, and I will do the same; and whichever of us God grants the victory, may Saint Peter add his blessing."

The Knight of the White Moon had been seen from the city, and word was sent to the viceroy that he was in conversation with Don Quixote. The viceroy, supposing it must be some fresh prank arranged by Don Antonio Moreno or some other gentleman of the city, hurried out at once to the beach with Don Antonio and several other gentlemen, just as Don Quixote was wheeling Rocinante round to take up the necessary distance. The viceroy, seeing that the pair were clearly preparing to charge, put himself between them and asked what had led them to engage in combat so suddenly. The Knight of the White Moon replied that it was a question of precedence in beauty, and briefly told him what he had said to Don Quixote, and how the conditions of the challenge had been accepted on both sides. The viceroy went over to Don Antonio and asked in a low voice whether he knew who the Knight of the White Moon was, or whether it was some joke they were playing on Don Quixote. Don Antonio replied that he neither knew who he was nor whether the challenge was in joke or in earnest. This answer left the viceroy unsure whether he ought to let the combat go on or not; but unable to persuade himself that it was anything but a joke, he fell back, saying, "If there is no other way out of this, gallant knights, except to confess or die, and Don Quixote is inflexible, and your worship of the White Moon still more so, then in God's hand be it — fall on."

The Knight of the White Moon thanked the viceroy in courteous and well-chosen words for the permission he gave them, and so did Don Quixote, who then, commending himself with all his heart to heaven and to his Dulcinea, as was his custom on the eve of any combat, proceeded to take a little more distance, since he saw his opponent was doing the same. Then, without trumpet blast or any other warlike instrument giving them the signal to charge, both at the same instant wheeled their horses; and the Knight of the White Moon, being the swifter, met Don Quixote two-thirds of the way through the course and there encountered him with such violence that, without touching him with his lance (which he held high, evidently on purpose), he hurled Don Quixote and Rocinante to the ground — a perilous fall. He sprang on him at once, and placing the lance over his visor said to him, "You are vanquished, sir knight — nay, dead, unless you admit the conditions of our challenge."

Don Quixote, bruised and stunned, without raising his visor, said in a weak feeble voice, as if he were speaking out of a tomb, "Dulcinea del Toboso is the fairest woman in the world, and I the most unfortunate knight on earth; it is not fitting that this truth should suffer for my weakness. Drive your lance home, sir knight, and take my life, since you have taken away my honour."

"That I will not, truly," said the Knight of the White Moon; "let the fame of the lady Dulcinea's beauty live on undimmed. All I require is that the great Don Quixote retire to his own home for a year, or for as long a time as I shall enjoin upon him, as we agreed before engaging in this combat."

The viceroy, Don Antonio, and several others who were present heard all this, and heard too how Don Quixote replied that so long as nothing in prejudice of Dulcinea was demanded of him, he would observe all the rest like a true and loyal knight. With that pledge given, the Knight of the White Moon wheeled about, bowed his head to the viceroy, and rode away into the city at a half gallop. The viceroy told Don Antonio to hurry after him and find out by some means or other who he was. They lifted Don Quixote up and uncovered his face, finding him pale and bathed in sweat.

Rocinante, from the hard treatment he had received, lay unable to stir for the moment. Sancho, wholly dejected and woebegone, did not know what to say or do. He fancied that all of this was a dream, that the whole business was a piece of enchantment. Here was his master defeated, and bound not to take up arms for a year. He saw the light of the glory of his achievements darkened, and the hopes of the recent promises swept away like smoke before the wind; Rocinante, he feared, was crippled for life, and his master's bones out of joint — and if he were only shaken out of his madness, that would be no small luck. In the end they carried him into the city in a hand-chair which the viceroy sent for, and the viceroy himself returned too, eager to find out who this Knight of the White Moon was who had left Don Quixote in such a sad plight.
